tldr: Addressing the vulnerability of VLA policies to visual noise and initial pose shifts, this work significantly improves runtime robustness without retraining the policy by retrieving and blending appropriate geometric motions from a motion primitive graph constructed from training trajectories at test time.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of R2A. Offline, successful demonstrations are structured into a graph using purely kinematic information. During execution, a sequential pipeline performs initial pose rectification via a diffusion model, dynamic retrieval of geometric motion primitives via a GNN, and harmonization (blending) with the policy's output via a gating mechanism.
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved remarkable semantic generalization through pre-training on large-scale datasets. However, they remain extremely vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) visual shifts—such as subtle changes in camera angles, lighting, or background textures—often causing the robot to deviate significantly from safe trajectories even when it understands the instructions. Collecting data to cover all infinite variations in real-world environments for finetuning is impractical. Furthermore, existing test-time adaptation methods that attempt to suppress spurious visual cues overlook the rich, uncorrupted motion patterns (kinematic priors) already embedded in the policy's own training experience.

To address this, the authors propose "Retrieve to Act (R2A)," a novel test-time scaling framework that formulates OOD robustness purely as a geometric motion primitive retrieval problem without relying on fragile visual features. First, successful training demonstrations are structured offline into an explicit spatiotemporal motion primitive graph with all visual features stripped away, where nodes represent kinematic states and displacements, and edges denote spatiotemporal transitions. During inference, a query-dependent Graph Neural Network (GNN) localizes the robot's ongoing execution within the graph using the execution history and VLA predictions, retrieving structurally compatible future motion primitives. These are then adaptively integrated with the frozen VLA's predicted actions via a learned dimension-wise gating mechanism, rectifying trajectory deviations while preserving local reactivity.

Evaluations across three state-of-the-art VLA architectures—GR00T N1.7, $\pi_{0.5}$, and StableVLA—in simulation benchmarks (LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin2.0-Plus) and on an Aloha real-world robot demonstrate absolute success rate improvements of up to +12% in simulation and +40% in real-world deployments, without requiring any finetuning of the base policies.
contributions: Proposing a method to structure past successful demonstrations into a spatiotemporal graph composed purely of kinematic information, bypassing fragile visual features.
Developing an initial state rectification mechanism using a diffusion model, alongside a query-dependent GNN to localize ongoing execution and retrieve future motion primitives.
Designing an adaptive dimension-wise gating mechanism that smoothly harmonizes (blends) retrieved geometric priors with the frozen VLA's action predictions.
Demonstrating substantial gains in robustness against perturbations across multiple state-of-the-art VLA models, bimanual manipulation, and real-world environments without any retraining.

sections.heading: Rescuing VLAs that Know "What to Do" but Lose "How to Move"
sections.summary: While VLAs excel at semantic task understanding, visual out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts frequently disrupt their physical trajectory generation. This paper presents R2A, a test-time adaptation framework that retrieves and leverages the geometric structure of successful training trajectories.
sections.details:
VLA models are adept at understanding the semantic goal of a task, yet they suffer from kinematic fragility: minor changes in camera perspective, background, or illumination can send the end-effector veering off course. In essence, the policy knows what needs to be achieved, but misleading visual noise causes it to lose track of how to physically move the arm.

Collecting perturbation data to finetune policies has clear limits, as it cannot cover the long-tail variations of real-world environments. Meanwhile, existing test-time methods that adjust visual attention overlook a valuable asset: correct, successful demonstration trajectories already exist within the training data.

A natural instinct might be to simply retrieve past demonstrations, but basic similarity searches fall short. Robot actions are not static snapshot observations; they form a highly structured spatiotemporal continuum.

To bridge this gap, the paper introduces "Retrieve to Act (R2A)." R2A completely discards visual features and builds a spatiotemporal "motion primitive graph" solely using kinematic information from training data (joint positions, end-effector poses, and state displacements). During inference, a query-dependent Graph Neural Network (GNN) localizes the ongoing execution within the graph, retrieves structurally compatible geometric motion primitives, and harmonizes them with the VLA's output. This achieves exceptional robustness against visual OOD perturbations without updating the base model's weights.

sections.heading: Shifting from Visual Test-Time Adaptation to Pure Kinematic Graph Retrieval
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work on test-time VLA robustness and retrieval-augmented robot learning, highlighting R2A's unique approach: searching an explicit, purely kinematic graph rather than relying on visual feature matching or external VLMs.
sections.details:
Related work broadly falls into three categories:

### Test-Time Robustness for VLA Policies
Approaches like BYOVLA erase irrelevant image regions via inpainting, VLS steers trajectories using reward functions generated by external VLMs, and SDN penalizes predictions close to failure trajectories. However, these methods depend on heavy visual modules and remain susceptible to visual noise.

### Retrieval-Augmented Robot Learning
Frameworks like RAM maintain past experiences in external memory and reuse them based on affordance similarity or trajectory conditioning. However, they rely on static matching between isolated observations and fail to capture the continuous spatiotemporal geometry of motion.

### Graph-Structured and Relational Retrieval
Techniques such as FlowRetrieval embed optical flow in latent spaces, while CLASS uses motion similarity as a contrastive objective during pre-training. Nevertheless, they remain tied to visual inputs or are not designed for online test-time retrieval.

The decisive advantage of R2A lies in completely eliminating fragile pixels and constructing an explicit topological graph using pure kinematic states. By directly tracking the geometric context of ongoing trajectories via a GNN, it achieves reliable motion primitive retrieval even under severe visual perturbations.

sections.heading: Inside R2A: Graph Construction, Initial Pose Rectification, and Dynamic GNN Retrieval
sections.summary: This section details R2A's core algorithm: building a pure kinematic graph from demonstrations, rectifying initial pose shifts with a diffusion model, and dynamically localizing and aggregating motion primitives via a query-dependent GNN.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
A robot's kinematic state consists of joint angles $\mathbf{q}_{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{7}$, forward-kinematics end-effector pose $\mathbf{x}_{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{6}$, and gripper state $\gamma_{t} \in \{0, 1\}$. Given images and language instructions, the frozen VLA policy $\pi$ outputs a $C$-step action chunk $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\pi}$. This is decoupled into continuous spatial pose commands $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\pi,\rm pose}$ and discrete gripper commands $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\pi,\rm grip}$. Since visual OOD shifts primarily corrupt spatial poses, R2A focuses on rectifying these trajectories via retrieval.

### 3.2 Overall Framework
The pipeline comprises four stages: (1) offline construction of the motion primitive graph, (2) initial state rectification at episode start, (3) dynamic GNN retrieval during execution, and (4) action harmonization.

### 3.3 Motion Primitive Graph Construction
A graph $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$ is constructed from demonstration dataset $\mathcal{D}$.
- **Node Representation**: Consecutive demonstration steps form nodes. Visual features are completely discarded; initial node features $\mathbf{h}_{v}^{(0)}$ concatenate normalized joint positions, displacements, gripper states, and positional encodings $\operatorname{PE}(\bar{s}_{v})$ of relative progress. Task labels $y_v$ and normalized progress scores $p_v \in [0, 1]$ serve as node metadata.
- **Edge Structure**: Temporal edges $\mathcal{E}_{\text{temp}}$ connect nodes forward in time within the same demonstration ($\Delta \in \{2, 4, 6, 8\}$), while spatial edges $\mathcal{E}_{\text{spatial}}$ link kinematically adjacent nodes across different demonstrations throughout the dataset.

### 3.4 Rectified Initial State via Diffusion
VLAs often fail immediately when the initial arm configuration deviates from the training distribution. A conditional diffusion model $\mathcal{M}_{\phi}$ takes the OOD initial pose $\mathbf{q}_{0}^{\rm OOD}$ and language instruction $\ell$ to generate a rectified pose $\mathbf{q}_{0}^{\rm rect}$ aligned with demonstration initial states. A smooth rigid-body trajectory moves the arm there before task execution begins.

### 3.5 Dynamic Retrieval via Query-Dependent GNN
During execution, VLA-predicted poses $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\pi,\rm pose}$ and recent kinematic history are encoded into a query $Q_t$. The GNN's message-passing layers are directly conditioned on $Q_t$, propagating task-relevant signals across the graph and assigning relevance scores $w_v$ to each node. Marginalization over $w_v$ produces estimated task probabilities $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_t$ and execution progress $\hat{p}_t$, updating the query into a context-aware $\tilde{Q}_t$ to re-rank and extract the Top-$K$ nodes. Finally, a weighted average of future demonstration actions yields the reference action $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\rm ref}$. The GNN is trained using a composite loss combining binary cross-entropy and a margin-based ranking loss on spatiotemporal positive neighbors.

sections.heading: Adaptive Gating: Seamlessly Blending Geometric Priors Only When Needed
sections.summary: This section describes how the retrieved geometric reference action is combined with the VLA's prediction. A learned dimension-wise gating mechanism pulls the trajectory toward the retrieval prior when the VLA errs, while preserving VLA flexibility during normal execution.
sections.details:
Directly playing back the retrieved reference action $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\rm ref}$ open-loop fails in dynamically varying environments. The robot must retain the VLA's closed-loop reactivity—such as adjusting to fine object offsets—while correcting catastrophic spatial drift caused by OOD shifts.

R2A solves this with an MLP that estimates a dimension-wise gating matrix $\mathbf{S}_{t} \in [0, 1]^{C \times 6}$:

$$\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\rm exec,\rm pose} = (\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{S}_{t}) \odot \mathbf{A}_{t}^{\pi,\rm pose} + \mathbf{S}_{t} \odot \mathbf{A}_{t}^{\rm ref}$$

where $\odot$ denotes the element-wise Hadamard product. The gripper command $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\pi,\rm grip}$ is executed directly without modification.

### Training the Harmonization Module
The MLP is trained with both the base VLA and the GNN frozen. During training, artificial noise $\epsilon$ is injected into kinematic queries to simulate visual perturbations. By minimizing the Mean Squared Error (MSE) against ground-truth demonstration trajectories, the MLP parameters $\theta$ learn an adaptive behavior: when VLA predictions deviate under noise, the gate $\mathbf{S}_{t}$ increases reliance on the reference action $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\rm ref}$; when predictions are accurate, it allows the VLA's actions to pass through.

sections.heading: Simulation and Real-World Experiments: Striking Robustness to Visual and Pose Shifts
sections.summary: Evaluations on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin2.0-Plus, and an Aloha robot show substantial robustness gains across GR00T N1.7, π0.5, and StableVLA, consistently outperforming existing test-time adaptation baselines.
sections.details:
### Key Findings
- **Q1. Does R2A improve base VLA robustness?**: On LIBERO-Plus across seven perturbation axes (viewpoint, initial pose, instruction, illumination, background, sensor noise, and layout), average success rates increased from 77.1% to 89.0% for GR00T N1.7, 78.1% to 89.5% for StableVLA, and 85.9% to 90.4% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Under robot initial state shifts, improvements were especially dramatic: +49.1% for GR00T and +48.0% for StableVLA. In the bimanual benchmark RoboTwin2.0-Plus, $\pi_{0.5}$'s success rate rose from 56.8% to 66.2% overall (and from 34.2% to 75.9% under initial pose perturbations).
- **Q2. Comparison with prior OOD baselines**: Compared to negative-conditioned guidance (SDN) and VLM-based reward steering (VLS), R2A achieved the highest overall success rate. Because SDN and VLS rely on visual object cues, they falter under camera shifts or robot pose deviations; R2A avoids this failure mode by directly retrieving geometric positive priors.
- **Q3. Real-world validation (Mobile ALOHA)**: Tested on Banana2Pot (place a banana in a pot and cover with lid) and Cube2Drawer (open drawer, place cube inside, close drawer). Under significant initial pose shifts, the success rate on Cube2Drawer jumped from 10% (baseline) to 45%.

### Ablation Studies and Inference Latency
Ablation experiments confirm that replacing the GNN retrieval with simple cosine similarity drops the success rate from 77.1% to 63.8%. Disabling action harmonization and directly executing retrieved actions collapses performance to just 1.2%. Rectified Initial State (RIS) proves vital, driving the success rate under initial pose perturbations from 49.9% up to 87.5%.
In terms of inference latency, R2A incurs minimal overhead (159 ms compared to the 138 ms baseline). This makes it far more viable for real-time control than VLS (>800 ms due to multi-view VLM queries) or SDN (which requires real-time instance segmentation).

captions.F2: Initial pose perturbation in real-world deployment (Banana2Pot task). Compared to the standard initial pose (top), R2A successfully recovers when the arm is initialized in an extreme offset position (bottom) through geometric rectification and retrieval.
captions.F3: Action correction under visual sensor noise (GR00T N1.7). Visual noise causes the raw policy prediction to float upward, but GNN retrieval identifies a demonstration descending toward the book, blending the trajectory into a correct 3.5 cm downward motion.

sections.heading: Looking Forward: New Horizons for VLAs Powered by Geometric Priors
sections.summary: This section summarizes the power of pure kinematic graph retrieval for overcoming visual OOD shifts, while discussing limitations such as the lack of explicit 3D scene geometry and autonomous recovery from unvisited failure states.
sections.details:
This work demonstrates that structuring successful training demonstrations into a kinematic graph and retrieving/harmonizing them at test time provides a powerful defense against visual perturbations in VLA policies.

The authors outline several limitations and promising directions for future research:
- **Lack of explicit scene geometry**: Because the retrieval index omits environment geometry (such as obstacles), the robot must rely on the VLA's vision to navigate newly placed obstacles. Grounding retrieval with multi-view spatial representations could address this.
- **Unseen failure recovery**: If the robot drifts into an unvisited failure state not covered in the demonstration graph, it cannot autonomously generate recovery behaviors.
- **Long-horizon task dependencies**: In non-Markovian environments with complex subtask transitions, integrating object-centric memory or semantic graph planners could allow retrieval conditioned on extended temporal contexts.
- **Alignment with human preferences**: Post-training alignment between human reference motions and geometric priors could jointly optimize task safety and operational preferences.

sections.heading: Appendix: Paired Analysis and Qualitative Execution Insights
sections.summary: Paired evaluations across identical seeds and perturbations quantify how many baseline failures R2A successfully "fixed." Step-by-step visualizations in LIBERO-Plus further illustrate R2A's corrective behavior.
sections.details:
### Detailed Paired Outcomes
Directly comparing GR00T N1.7 against R2A under identical random seeds, tasks, and perturbation settings reveals that R2A "fixed" base model failures in 229 episodes under initial pose perturbations, 133 episodes under sensor noise, and 101 episodes under camera viewpoint changes. Conversely, episodes broken by R2A were minimal, yielding a substantial net gain.
As perturbation severity increased (e.g., larger arm offset angles), the baseline's success rate collapsed from 82% to 11%, whereas R2A retained strong resilience, shifting only from 93% to 81%.

### Qualitative Rollout Analysis
In a camera-shift scenario, the standalone VLA continually pushed the soup container after placement and failed to transition to picking up the cheese. R2A retrieved a demonstration segment at step 104 that "opened the gripper and ascended," smoothly steering the robot back into the correct multi-stage sequence. Under severe initial pose offsets, R2A rectified the arm position before accurately retrieving reach-to-mug primitives to complete the task.

captions.F5: Paired evaluation outcomes on LIBERO-Plus. (a) Across all perturbation axes, the proportion of episodes fixed by R2A (blue) overwhelmingly exceeds broken episodes (orange). (b) Heatmap showing success rate gains across individual tasks.
captions.F8: Qualitative rollout comparisons on LIBERO-Long. Under both camera viewpoint shifts (top) and initial pose shifts (bottom), the standalone VLA (red) fails mid-execution, whereas R2A (green) retrieves compatible demonstrations (blue) to correct motion and successfully achieve the task goal.

takeaways: VLA vulnerability to visual OOD shifts stems from losing spatial motion guidance rather than losing semantic task comprehension; directly reusing past kinematic structures provides a highly effective remedy.
Constructing a graph entirely devoid of visual pixels—using only joint positions and end-effector poses—creates an impervious buffer against visual noise.
Rather than naively replaying retrieved actions, adaptively blending them via dimension-wise gating based on prediction discrepancies preserves both local reactivity and global stability.
Substantial robustness gains are achieved without finetuning base policy weights, requiring only a lightweight test-time inference module (+0.37M parameters, +21 ms latency).
limitations: The retrieval index lacks explicit obstacle and object geometry, meaning novel obstacle avoidance still relies entirely on the base VLA's visual perception.
The framework cannot autonomously synthesize recovery behaviors when the robot falls into completely unprecedented failure states absent from the demonstration graph.
Because the harmonization module is trained using synthetic noise, unmodeled, catastrophic prediction failures could lead to inaccurate gating decisions.
